metadata.title: An Elementary Proof of a Theorem of Johnson and Lindenstrauss
metadata.source_note: Extracted from PDF->text fallback; .tex source not available. Math fidelity reduced.

nodes.name: Johnson-Lindenstrauss Theorem (this paper's version)
nodes.statement: For any $0 < \epsilon < 1$ and integer $n$, let $k$ be a positive integer with $k \geq 4(\epsilon^2/2 - \epsilon^3/3)^{-1} \ln n$. Then for any set $V$ of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, there is a map $f : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^k$ such that for all $u, v \in V$, $(1-\epsilon)\|u-v\|^2 \leq \|f(u)-f(v)\|^2 \leq (1+\epsilon)\|u-v\|^2$. Furthermore, this map can be found in randomized polynomial time.
nodes.statement_clean: Any n points in R^d can be mapped to R^k with k = O(log n / epsilon^2) such that pairwise squared distances are preserved within factor (1 +/- epsilon), and the map is found in randomized polynomial time.
conclusions: There exists $f : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^k$ with $(1-\epsilon)\|u-v\|^2 \leq \|f(u)-f(v)\|^2 \leq (1+\epsilon)\|u-v\|^2$ for all $u,v \in V$
$f$ is found in randomized polynomial time

nodes.name: Johnson-Lindenstrauss Theorem (original)
nodes.statement: Any $n$-point subset of Euclidean space can be embedded in $k = O(\log n / \epsilon^2)$ dimensions without distorting pairwise distances by more than a factor of $(1 \pm \epsilon)$, for any $0 < \epsilon < 1$.
conclusions: Embedding into $k = O(\log n / \epsilon^2)$ dimensions exists with distortion $(1 \pm \epsilon)$

nodes.name: Concentration of projected length (Lemma 2.2)
nodes.statement: Let $k < d$. (a) If $\beta < 1$, then $\Pr[L \leq \beta k / d] \leq \beta^{k/2} \big(1 + (1-\beta)k/(d-k)\big)^{(d-k)/2} \leq \exp\big((k/2)(1 - \beta + \ln \beta)\big)$. (b) If $\beta > 1$, then $\Pr[L \geq \beta k / d] \leq \beta^{k/2} \big(1 + (1-\beta)k/(d-k)\big)^{(d-k)/2} \leq \exp\big((k/2)(1 - \beta + \ln \beta)\big)$.
nodes.statement_clean: The squared length L of the projection of a uniformly random unit vector onto the first k coordinates is sharply concentrated around its mean k/d.
assumptions: $Z$ is the projection of $Y$ onto its first $k$ coordinates

nodes.name: Random unit vector via Gaussian normalization
nodes.statement: Let $X_1, \ldots, X_d$ be i.i.d. $N(0,1)$ random variables, and let $Y = (X_1, \ldots, X_d) / \|X\|$. Then $Y$ is uniformly distributed on the surface $S^{d-1}$ of the $d$-dimensional sphere.

nodes.name: Projection L and its mean
nodes.statement: Let $Z \in \mathbb{R}^k$ be the projection of $Y$ onto its first $k$ coordinates and let $L = \|Z\|^2$. Then $\mu = E[L] = k/d$.

nodes.name: Equivalent form of Lemma 2.2(a) inequality (2.2)
nodes.statement: $\Pr[d(X_1^2 + \cdots + X_k^2) \leq k\beta(X_1^2 + \cdots + X_d^2)] \leq \beta^{k/2} \big(1 + k(1-\beta)/(d-k)\big)^{(d-k)/2}$

nodes.name: Gaussian moment generating function
nodes.statement: If $X \sim N(0,1)$, then $E[e^{sX^2}] = 1/\sqrt{1 - 2s}$ for $-\infty < s < 1/2$.

nodes.name: Optimal t in MGF minimization
nodes.statement: $t_0 = (1 - \beta) / (2\beta(d - k\beta))$ minimizes $g(t) = (1 - 2tk\beta)^{-(d-k)/2}(1 - 2t(k\beta - d))^{-k/2}$ over $0 < t < 1/(2k\beta)$.

nodes.name: Logarithmic inequalities used in proof
nodes.statement: $\ln(1 - x) \leq -x - x^2/2$ for $0 \leq x < 1$; and $\ln(1 + x) \leq x - x^2/2 + x^3/3$ for $x \geq 0$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.1 (JL Theorem)
nodes.statement: Project the points onto a random $k$-dimensional subspace, apply Lemma 2.2 to bound the probability that any pair's distance is distorted by more than $(1\pm\epsilon)$, then use a union bound and rescale by $f(v_i) = \sqrt{d/k}\,v'_i$.

nodes.name: Set up random projection
nodes.statement: If $d \leq k$ the theorem is trivial. Otherwise take a random $k$-dimensional subspace $S$ and let $v'_i$ be the projection of $v_i \in V$ into $S$. Set $L = \|v'_i - v'_j\|^2$ and $\mu = (k/d)\|v_i - v_j\|^2$.

nodes.name: Lower-tail bound via Lemma 2.2(a)
nodes.statement: Apply Lemma 2.2(a) with $\beta = 1 - \epsilon$ and use $\ln(1-x) \leq -x - x^2/2$ to get $\Pr[L \leq (1 - \epsilon)\mu] \leq \exp(-k\epsilon^2/4) \leq \exp(-2 \ln n) = 1/n^2$.

nodes.name: Upper-tail bound via Lemma 2.2(b)
nodes.statement: Apply Lemma 2.2(b) with $\beta = 1 + \epsilon$ and use $\ln(1+x) \leq x - x^2/2 + x^3/3$ to get $\Pr[L \geq (1 + \epsilon)\mu] \leq \exp(-k(\epsilon^2/2 - \epsilon^3/3)/2) \leq 1/n^2$.

nodes.name: Union bound and rescaling
nodes.statement: Set $f(v_i) = \sqrt{d/k}\,v'_i$. For a fixed pair, distortion fails to lie in $[1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon]$ with probability $\leq 2/n^2$. By the union bound over $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs, the failure probability is at most $1 - 1/n$, so $f$ has the desired properties with probability $\geq 1/n$. Repeating the projection $O(n)$ times boosts success probability to a constant.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.2(a)
nodes.statement: Use the Gaussian MGF $E[e^{sX^2}] = 1/\sqrt{1-2s}$, apply Markov's inequality to an exponentiated linear combination of $X_i^2$, then minimize the resulting bound over the parameter $t$.

nodes.name: Rewrite via exponentiation and Markov
nodes.statement: $\Pr[d(X_1^2+\cdots+X_k^2) \leq k\beta(X_1^2+\cdots+X_d^2)] = \Pr[\exp\{t(k\beta(X_1^2+\cdots+X_d^2) - d(X_1^2+\cdots+X_k^2))\} \geq 1] \leq E[\exp\{\cdots\}]$ for $t > 0$, by Markov's inequality.

nodes.name: Compute the MGF using independence
nodes.statement: By independence, $E[\exp\{\cdots\}] = E[\exp(tk\beta X^2)]^{d-k}\,E[\exp(t(k\beta - d)X^2)]^k = (1 - 2tk\beta)^{-(d-k)/2}(1 - 2t(k\beta - d))^{-k/2} =: g(t)$, valid for $0 < t < 1/(2k\beta)$.

nodes.name: Optimize over t
nodes.statement: Minimize $g(t)$ by maximizing $f(t) = (1 - 2tk\beta)^{d-k}(1 - 2t(k\beta - d))^k$ on $(0, 1/(2k\beta))$. The maximum is at $t_0 = (1-\beta)/(2\beta(d-k\beta))$, giving $f(t_0) = ((d - k\beta)/(d - k))^{d-k} (1/\beta)^k$, and $g(t_0) = 1/\sqrt{f(t_0)}$ proves inequality (2.2).

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.2(b)
nodes.statement: The proof is almost exactly the same as that of Lemma 2.2(a). The same calculations show $\Pr[d(X_1^2+\cdots+X_k^2) \geq k\beta(X_1^2+\cdots+X_d^2)] \leq (1 + 2tk\beta)^{-(d-k)/2}(1 + 2t(k\beta - d))^{-k/2} = g(-t)$ for $0 < t < 1/(2(d - k\beta))$, minimized at $-t_0$, which lies in the desired range for $\beta > 1$.

nodes.name: Comparison with Indyk-Motwani and Achlioptas
nodes.statement: Indyk-Motwani [12] use $k$ independent random Gaussian vectors $\{U_i\}$ and set the $i$-th coordinate of $f(x)$ to $\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\langle U_i, x \rangle$; their analogue of Lemma 2.2 is weaker by an additive $O(\log\log n)$ in $k$, but the algorithm is simpler. Achlioptas [2] further shows the entries of $A$ may be drawn uniformly from $\{+1, -1\}$ and recovers the same bound for $k$ as Theorem 2.1.

nodes.name: Tightness via Alon
nodes.statement: Alon has shown the JL bound is essentially tight: any set of $n$ points with inter-point distances in $[1 - \epsilon, 1 + \epsilon]$ requires at least $\Omega(\log n / (\epsilon^2 \log(1/\epsilon)))$ dimensions.
nodes.origin_citation: Alon, Problems and results in extremal combinatorics, Part I
